region.text: the five disputed regions of Quảng Nguyên, most of modern Cao Bằng and Lạng Sơn

ledger.note: 1082: the Song return Quang Nguyen. The Song 'relinquished its control of four prefectures and the county of Dai Viet', 'including the Nung clan's home of Quang Nguyen' (re-opened); the talks of July-August 1084 fixed the Quang Nguyen-Guihua border. Added after review (mirror of the ngo-dynasty gain).

region.text: the Ordos plateau and Lanzhou

ledger.note: April 1085: war ends with Shenzong's death. 'In exchange for 100 Chinese prisoners, the Song returned four of the six captured towns'; the page does not name them, so no loss region is recorded. Hostilities resumed five years later; the Song built 40 forts on the Ordos 1097-1099 and the 1099 peace left the border undemarcated.

region.text: Qingtang, renamed Xining, annexed from Tsongkha in 1103

ledger.note: 1103: the Song annex the Tsongkha kingdom. 'In 1103 the Song dispatched Wang Hou to conquer Tsongkha ... the Song armies occupied the region again and renamed Qingtang to Xining'; resistance was suppressed in 1104 (Song-Xia wars page). Tsongkha infobox: disestablished 1104.

region.text: Qingtang, renamed Xining, annexed from Tsongkha in 1103

ledger.note: 1113: the Xia 'took the Qingtang region' (Song-Xia wars page), but the Tsongkha page has the Song prince Zhao Huaide in 1108 and the Jin ceding the area to the Xia only in 1136; the pages disagree, so the land is not removed from the Song keyframes. Confidence 1 for the loss. Re-opened after review: the Song-Xia wars page says 'the Western Xia started building fortifications in disputed territory' and 'took the Qingtang region' in 1113 and names no later Song recovery; the Tsongkha page (1103 Song, 1108 Zhao Huaide, 1136 Jin cession to Xia) is not reconciled with it, so the gap stays open.

region.text: the Sixteen Prefectures round Yanjing 'except Yunzhou'

ledger.note: 1123: the Jin hand Yanjing and the Sixteen Prefectures to the Song. 'In 1123 the Jin ceded most of the territories except Yunzhou to the Song'; the Jin-Song wars page: 'In May 1123 Tong Guan and the Song armies entered the looted Yanjing'. The counterpart is the Jin, whose dossier starts in 1115 (Liao land).

region.text: the Sixteen Prefectures round Yanjing 'except Yunzhou'

ledger.note: 1125: the Jin retake the Sixteen Prefectures in their invasion. The prefectures were 'retaken in an invasion of Song territory in 1125' (Sixteen Prefectures page).

region.text: Hebei and Shanxi, 'occupied' by the Jurchens 'within a few months' of the autumn 1125 invasion

ledger.note: November 1125: the Jin invade. 'In November 1125 Taizong ordered his armies to attack the Song'; the Jurchens reached the Yellow River on 27 January 1126 and besieged Kaifeng on 31 January.

region.text: Hebei and Shanxi, 'occupied' by the Jurchens 'within a few months' of the autumn 1125 invasion

ledger.note: 1126: Hebei and Shanxi pass to the Jin. 'The Jin had occupied most of Shanxi and Hebei' within a few months of the autumn 1125 invasion (Jin page); the first siege of Kaifeng was lifted on 10 February 1126 after 33 days. The page gives no day for the occupation.

region.text: Hebei and Shanxi, 'occupied' by the Jurchens 'within a few months' of the autumn 1125 invasion

ledger.note: 1126: the Jin hold Hebei and Shanxi; the fighting moves to the Yellow River and Henan.

1127: the Northern Song ends and the Southern Song begins. The Song page's capitals run Bianjing (960-1127), then Yingtian, Yangzhou, Lin'an; Gaozong was enthroned at Yingtianfu on 12 June 1127 (Jin-Song wars page). Same state and colour; Cliopatria's Southern Song row begins in 1139.

region.text: the Yellow River plain and Shaanxi between the Yellow River and the Qinling-Huai line, fought over by Song, Jin and Jin's puppets Chu and Qi

ledger.note: 9 January 1127: Kaifeng falls. 'On January 9, 1127, the Jurchens broke through and started to loot the conquered city'; Qinzong and the Huizong court were taken in the Jingkang Incident. Henan, Shandong and Shaanxi become the contested zone between the Song, the Jin and the puppets Chu (1127) and Qi (1130-1137) until the 1142 treaty. Great Chu (Zhang Bangchang, 20 April-23 May 1127) is not given a Song loss and gain: its Kaifeng disc lies inside this contested zone and a one-month puppet is below the one-year step (exception, see notes).
12 June 1127: Gaozong is enthroned at Yingtianfu (Shangqiu), then moves to Yangzhou in late 1127 or early 1128 and flees south of the Yangtze in 1129.

region.text: the Yangtze delta and Zhejiang: Hangzhou and Shaoxing

ledger.note: December 1129: Wuzhu's armies cross the Huai. 'In December 1129, the Jin started a new military offensive, dispatching two armies across the Huai River'; they 'seized Hangzhou (January 22, 1130) and then Shaoxing further south (February 4)'.

region.text: the Yangtze delta and Zhejiang

ledger.note: 1130: the Jin raid ends. 'Soon, the Jurchens gave up the pursuit and retreated north' (Gaozong page); the Jin created Da Qi in 1130 to rule the Yellow River plain.

union.text: Hezhou (Linxia) with Wushengjun/Xizhou, taken from the Tsongkha lords in 1072
Lanzhou, taken from Western Xia in October 1081
Qingtang, renamed Xining, annexed from Tsongkha in 1103

minus.text: Hebei and Shanxi, 'occupied' by the Jurchens 'within a few months' of the autumn 1125 invasion
the 1126 shape (with the north-west gains) minus Hebei and Shanxi; Henan, Shandong and Shaanxi are drawn as contested with the Jin from January 1127
Cliopatria's 1139 Southern Song shape, i.e. the land south of the Qinling-Huai line

region.text: the land north of the Qinling-Huai line lost in 1127-1130: Henan, Shandong, Shaanxi, eastern Gansu, the Huai-north strip of Jiangsu and Anhui, and the Linxia, Lanzhou and Xining discs

ledger.note: Late 1130: the Song lose the land north of the Qinling-Huai line to the Jin. 'Da Qi was formed late in 1130, and the Jin enthroned Liu as its emperor'; Zhang Jun 'was defeated by Wuzhu near Xi'an in late 1130' and Wuzhu 'advanced further west into Gansu' (re-opened). The pages give no line, so the lost land is the 1126-1129 shape minus Cliopatria's 1139 Southern Song shape (about 600 thousand km2 by the gazetteer; confidence 2). Added after review: the great-jin dossier records the matching gain and the split to great-qi.

region.text: Xiangyang and the prefectures round it on the Han river

ledger.note: November 1133: Qi invades the Song. 'With Jin support, Da Qi invaded the Song in November 1133'; the Han river front round Xiangyang. Qi (Liu Yu, 1130-1137) is a state Cliopatria lacks.

region.text: Xiangyang and its surrounding prefectures

ledger.note: 1134: Yue Fei retakes Xiangyang. 'In 1134, Yue Fei defeated Li and retook Xiangyang and its surrounding prefectures' (the Jin-Song wars page has the same sentence).

region.text: Xiangyang and its surrounding prefectures

ledger.note: 1134: the Xiangyang front closes with the recapture; Qi was abolished in late 1137.

1138: Lin'an (Hangzhou) is officially declared the capital. 'In 1138, Gaozong officially declared Lin'an the capital of the dynasty'; the page says Lin'an had replaced Kaifeng as temporary capital 'in 1133'.

region.text: the Yellow River plain and Shaanxi between the Yellow River and the Qinling-Huai line, fought over by Song, Jin and Jin's puppets Chu and Qi

ledger.note: 1139: the Jin return Henan and Shaanxi. They 'returned to the Song in 1139' (Jin page). The Jin-Song wars page says the 1138 treaty 'set the Yellow River as the border' but 'never came into effect'. Shandong stays Jin.

region.text: Henan and Shaanxi, returned by the Jin

ledger.note: 1139: the Song regain Henan and Shaanxi. The Gaozong page does not mention the return; the Jin page does.

region.text: Henan and Shaanxi, retaken by the Jin

ledger.note: 1140: the Jin retake the plain. 'In 1140, the Jin retook Shaanxi and Henan' (Jin page); the Jin-Song wars page: 'On July 8, 1140, at the Battle of Yancheng, Wuzhu launched a surprise attack on Song forces'.

region.text: Henan and Shaanxi, retaken by the Jin

ledger.note: 1140: the Jin retake Henan and Shaanxi. 'In 1140, the Jin retook Shaanxi and Henan and sent troops south of the Yellow River' (re-opened); the Jin-Song wars page has Wuzhu invade in early 1140. Added after review (mirror of the great-jin gain of 1140); the 1139 keyframe holds the two provinces for one year only.

region.text: Henan and Shaanxi

ledger.note: 11 October 1142: the Treaty of Shaoxing ends the fighting. 'The treaty was signed in 1141 ... formally ratified on 11 October 1142 when a Jin envoy visited the Song court'; the Jin page has the Huai border offered in October 1141 and the treaty 'finalized on 11 October 1142'.

minus.text: the Yellow River plain and Shaanxi between the Yellow River and the Qinling-Huai line, fought over by Song, Jin and Jin's puppets Chu and Qi

region.text: the lands north of the Qinling-Huai line

ledger.note: 1142: the Song give up the north. 'The Song renounced claims to former Northern Song lands north of the Qinling Huaihe Line, which included its former capital of Kaifeng'; they pay tribute of 250,000 taels of silver and 250,000 packs of silk to the 'suzerain Jin' as a 'quasi-tributary state' until 1164 (the vassal tint is recorded in the Jin ledger). After review: the Song kept none of this land after 1140 (loss of 1130 and 1140 above), so the event records the treaty's renunciation of claims and its region equals the great-jin gain of 1142.

region.text: the Huai river line, crossed by the Jin on 28 October 1161

ledger.note: October 1161: Wanyan Liang invades. He 'crossed the Huai on 28 October'; the Jin fleet lost at sea on 16 November (Tangdao); the army was beaten at Caishi on 26-27 November; Liang was murdered on 15 December 1161.

region.text: the Huai river line

ledger.note: 1165: peace restored. The Jin-Song wars page: hostilities 'subsided in 1165 after the negotiation of a peace treaty'; the Jin page names it the Treaty of Longxing, 1165.

region.text: the Huai river line

ledger.note: 1206: the Song go to war with the Jin. 'War against the Jin was officially declared on June 14, 1206'; Wu Xi defected to the Jin in December 1206. The declaration is the page's date; the first ground-taking campaign is not dated.

region.text: the Huai river line

ledger.note: 2 November 1208: peace. 'A peace treaty was signed on November 2, 1208, and the Song tribute to the Jin was reinstated'; Han Tuozhou had been killed on 24 November 1207.

region.text: Sichuan through the Chengdu plain and the Han river round Xiangyang

ledger.note: February 1235: the Mongol-Song war begins (infobox '11 February 1235 - 19 March 1279'). 'From 1235 on, the Mongol general Koden started to attack the region of Sichuan through the Chengdu plain.'

region.text: Xiangyang, defended by Cao Youwen

ledger.note: 1236: Xiangyang capitulates. 'Xiangyang, which was defended by the Song general Cao Youwen, capitulated in 1236'; the Song retook it in 1239 (page paraphrase).

region.text: Xiangyang

ledger.note: 1239: the Song retake Xiangyang. The page has Xiangyang changing hands in 1236-1239, 'the Song retook it in 1239'; Huai river area: the Mongols mostly stayed on the defensive.

region.text: the Chengdu plain

ledger.note: 1241: Chengdu falls. 'The only permanent gain was Chengdu for the Mongols in 1241'; the Mongols invaded Sichuan again in 1242.

region.text: the rest of western Sichuan

ledger.note: 1260: western Sichuan is Mongol in Cliopatria. The page dates no loss in 1260 (Mongke 'entered Sichuan in 1258' and died at Diaoyu on 11 August 1259; Kublai besieged Ezhou in November 1259 and was elected Great Khan in 1260); the year is the Cliopatria step. Re-opened after review: the Siege of Diaoyu Castle page has Diaoyu Castle 'remained in the hands of Song armies' after Mongke's death and covers nothing of 1260-1262; the Mongol conquest page names no Sichuan territory held in 1260. Still unverified.

region.text: Xiangyang and Fancheng on the Han river

ledger.note: 1268: the siege of Xiangyang begins. 'In 1268, the Mongol advance was halted at the city of Xiangyang, situated on the Han River'; the Song page: Kublai 'blockaded the Yangtze River and besieged Xiangyang' from 1268 to 1273.

region.text: Xiangyang and Fancheng

ledger.note: 1273: the Han river bastion falls. 'In 1273, Fancheng capitulated, the Mongols putting the entire population to death'; the page gives no date for Xiangyang itself.

region.text: Xiangyang and Fancheng

ledger.note: 1273: the Xiangyang siege ends; the Yangtze campaign of 1274-1276 follows (Changzhou massacred in 1275).

1276: the court flees south. The empress dowager sent the child emperor's two brothers to Fuzhou; Zhao Shi was enthroned as Duanzong 'far from the capital' and died in Guangdong; Zhao Bing was enthroned as Huaizong.

region.text: the Song south from the Yangtze to the Wuyi and Nanling mountains

ledger.note: February 1276: Lin'an surrenders. 'When Bayan and Dong Wenbing camped outside Lin'an in February 1276, the Song ... surrendered the underage Emperor Gong along with the imperial seal'; the Song page: 'By 1276, most of the Song territory had been captured by Yuan forces'. The region is the 1272 shape without Fujian and Guangdong (reading).

region.text: Chongqing

ledger.note: 1277: Chongqing falls: 'The strongholds of the Song loyalists fell one by one: Yangzhou in 1276, Chongqing in 1277 and Hezhou in 1279.'

region.text: the whole Song south, 1235-1279

ledger.note: 19 March 1279: the Mongol-Song war ends at Yamen (infobox '11 February 1235 - 19 March 1279').

region.text: the last fleet and the Guangdong coast

ledger.note: 19 March 1279: the Song end at Yamen. 'On 19 March 1279, the Mongols defeated the last of the Song forces at the naval Battle of Yamen'; the child emperor Zhao Bing 'committed suicide' (Southern Song page). Hezhou fell the same year.

wars.name: Song conquest of the Ten Kingdoms
wars.outcome: The Song annexed Jingnan and Hunan (963), Later Shu (965), the Southern Han (971), the Southern Tang (975/976), Wuyue (978) and the Northern Han (979).
wars.note: Years only on the page; the Song page adds a battle on 23 January 971 against the Southern Han.

wars.name: Song-Liao wars
wars.outcome: Song defeats at the Gaoliang River (979) and in the three-pronged invasion of 986; the Liao struck toward Kaifeng in 1004 and the Chanyuan Treaty of January 1005 fixed the border and set a yearly Song tribute.
wars.note: Gaoliang River 979 and the 986 campaign are dated by the Liao page; the Song page dates only 1005.

wars.name: Song-Xia war of 1038-1044
wars.outcome: Xia victories at Sanchuan Pass, Haoshuichuan and Dingchuan; peace in 1044 with the Song recognising the Xia ruler as king and paying 250,000 units of silk, silver and tea yearly.

wars.name: Song-Xia war of 1081-1085

union.text: the Ordos and Lanzhou

wars.outcome: The five-pronged Song attack took Lanzhou and other towns, then failed at the flooded Yellow River camps (21 December 1081); Yongle fell to the Xia in September 1082; four of six captured towns were returned in April 1085.
wars.note: The wars resumed 1097-1099 (40 Song forts on the Ordos), 1103-1105 (Tsongkha, Lanzhou, Qingtang) and 1113-1119 (Liu Fa's invasion; ceasefire and apology in 1119).

wars.name: Song conquest of Tsongkha
wars.outcome: Hezhou and Xizhou taken in 1072; submission of Dongzhan and Mucheng in 1074; Wang Hou's conquest of Tsongkha in 1103; Qingtang renamed Xining; resistance put down in 1104.

wars.name: Ly-Song War
wars.outcome: Ly Thuong Kiet took Qinzhou, Lianzhou and Yongzhou (1075-1076); the Song invasion of 1076-1077 was halted at the Nhu Nguyet River; Yong, Qin and Lian were returned in 1082 and the border fixed in 1084.

wars.name: Jin-Song wars (Jingkang and the Southern Song founding)

zones.text: Hebei and Shanxi, 'occupied' by the Jurchens 'within a few months' of the autumn 1125 invasion
the Yellow River plain and Shaanxi between the Yellow River and the Qinling-Huai line, fought over by Song, Jin and Jin's puppets Chu and Qi

wars.outcome: The Jin took Hebei and Shanxi (1126) and Kaifeng (9 January 1127), set up Chu (1127) and Qi (1130-1137), raided the Yangtze delta (December 1129-February 1130); Henan and Shaanxi were returned in 1139 and retaken in 1140; the Treaty of Shaoxing (ratified 11 October 1142) set the border at the Huai river and the Qinling and made the Song a tributary of the Jin.
wars.note: The pages opened do not give the 1130-1138 front line; fighting in 1131-1132 was in Shaanxi, Gansu and Sichuan.

wars.name: Jin-Song war of 1161
wars.outcome: Wanyan Liang crossed the Huai on 28 October 1161, lost at Tangdao (16 November) and Caishi (26-27 November) and was murdered on 15 December; peace (Longxing) in 1165.

wars.name: Jin-Song war of 1206-1208
wars.outcome: War declared 14 June 1206; peace signed 2 November 1208 and the Song tribute to the Jin reinstated.

wars.name: Song-Mongol alliance against the Jin
wars.outcome: The Song 'formed an alliance with the Mongols against the Jin' in 1233 and supplied them 'in return for parts of Henan'; the Jin ended on 9 February 1234. No Song gain in Henan is dated on the page.

wars.name: Mongol conquest of the Song dynasty
wars.outcome: Chengdu lost 1241; Mongke died at Diaoyu 11 August 1259; Xiangyang besieged 1268-1273; Lin'an surrendered February 1276; Chongqing fell 1277; the last Song fleet was destroyed at Yamen on 19 March 1279.

certainty.note: The unification campaigns and the Liao frontier before Chanyuan are approximate; provincial limits in the south follow prefectures.
The Liao frontier was 'finalized' by the Chanyuan Treaty (1005) and the Vietnamese frontier was fixed in 1084; the Xia, Tibetan and Dali frontiers stay soft.
A moving war front; the pages opened give no line for 1130-1138.
The Huai river and Qinling line set by the Treaty of Shaoxing (1142) was the Jin border until 1234; the frontier with the Dali and Tibetan lands stays soft.
The Mongol war front: Sichuan, the Han river and the Yangtze changed hands year by year.

notes:
One dossier for the whole Song: Cliopatria's 'Northern Song' (961-1138) and 'Southern Song' (1139-1278) share Wikidata Q7462 and are one dynasty and state (the court moved south of the Yangtze in 1127 and went on). The dossier takes the slug northern-song, lists both Names and reviews all twelve shapes; there is NO separate southern-song dossier (other dossiers cite 'southern-song' as a counterpart: read it as this dossier). The Song dossier runs 960-1279 where Cliopatria runs 961-1278.

Cliopatria problems: (1) the 1126-1138 shape (2.8 M km2) keeps the whole north although the Jin took Hebei and Shanxi in 1126 and Kaifeng on 9 January 1127; new keyframes give the shape minus Hebei and Shanxi (1126-1129) and Cliopatria's 1139 shape for 1130-1138 (the front line of 1130-1138 is not on any page opened). (2) The 1272 shape is repeated to 1278 although Xiangyang fell in 1273, Lin'an in February 1276 and Chongqing in 1277. (3) The unification of 963-979 is one step at 970 and one at 980; new keyframes follow the years. (4) The Lanzhou, Hezhou and Xining gains of 1072-1103 and the Yan gain of 1123-1125 are not in any shape; new keyframes add them.

Not settled: the pages opened do not give the Song-Jin front for 1130-1138 or the exact towns returned to the Xia in 1085; the Song-Xia wars page says the Xia took Qingtang in 1113 while the Tsongkha page has the Song there in 1108 and the Jin ceding the area in 1136; the Southern Tang's end is 975 or 976 on the same page; Zhou Xingfeng's Wuping (Hunan 963), Zhang Bangchang's Great Chu (1127) and Liu Yu's Great Qi (1130-1137) need dossiers; the Dali Kingdom was a nominal tributary from 982 (Dali page) and is not tinted here. Haoshuichuan is dated to the winter of 1039-1040 by the Song-Xia wars page (other accounts say 1041). The Mongol conquest of Dali (1253) is in the Dali dossier. Names the gazetteer lacks: 'Sixteen Prefectures' (rendered here as Beijing, Tianjin and a 80 km disc round Baoding).
Pages thin or off-point: Northern Song and Southern Song are redirects to Song dynasty; the Emperor Taizu page gives no campaign dates; the Treaty of Shaoxing page lacks Dasan Pass.

Fix round after review (2026-10-19): (1) Hunan was missing from the 965-975 shapes (the Cliopatria 970 shape holds none of it): added to the keyframes of 965-979. (2) The 976 gain of the Southern Tang and the 978 gains now follow the southern-tang, wuyue and qingyuan-circuit dossiers: corrected Southern Tang realm in 976; Wuyue with Fuzhou, and a new gain from qingyuan-circuit (Quanzhou, Zhangzhou) in 978. (3) New loss of 1130 (about 600 thousand km2 north of the Qinling-Huai line, region = the 1126-1129 shape minus Cliopatria's 1139 Southern Song shape) to the Jin, who split Qi from it; the K18 keyframe is Cliopatria's 1139 shape from 1130. (4) New loss of Henan and Shaanxi in 1140. The 1142 loss stays as the treaty's renunciation (its region equals the great-jin gain). (5) The Ly-Song war: the 1075 contest became the owner's occupation (1075-1082, as in ngo-dynasty), the contest is the Song invasion of 1076-1077 on the approach to Thang Long (as in ngo-dynasty), and Quang Nguyen (Cao Bang, Lang Son) is a gain of 1077 and a loss of 1082 with keyframes 1077-1081; the 1056 step is a Guangxi border adjustment, not Quang Nguyen. (6) Great Chu (20 April-23 May 1127): no Song loss/gain; the Kaifeng disc is inside the contested zone of 1127-01 and a one-month puppet is below the one-year step (exception allowed by the reviewer). Disagreements and unresolved: the 1113 loss of Qingtang (Song-Xia wars page: the Xia 'took the Qingtang region' in 1113; Tsongkha page: Jin cession to the Xia in 1136) is not reconciled, the keyframes keep the Xining disc Song until 1130 and Jin until 1136 on the Tsongkha reading; the 1260 loss of western Sichuan and the 1250 step stay unverified (Siege of Diaoyu Castle and Mongol conquest pages re-opened and silent); the Song 'gain' of 'parts of Henan' in 1233-1234 is not recorded: the Mongol conquest of the Jin page says only that the Song provided supplies 'in return for parts of Henan', and the Mongol conquest of the Song page has the Song advance to Kaifeng in 1234 and be 'completely repelled', so no land is shown changing hands. The Xiangyang events of 1236, 1239 and 1273 and the 1231 Shaanxi loss still lack a mirror in mongol-empire (ia-02).
